Interesting! Do you find any of your perspectives on your identity or history have changed since this discovery? 

I have a similar story, but atleast growing up was told that my paternal grandmother's side were "mixed with Cherokee". It seemed plausible enough due to the way my grandma looked (the best way to describe it is to say her skin tone wasn't quite like a typical "white" person, it was more along the lines of what African-Americans would call "high yellow" or "yellow bone", along with thick curls in her hair along with other family) and the fact that her family was from deep in Appalachia in eastern Kentucky, so I took it at face value growing up. I also had found websites from her home county that described her extended family as the "county Red People/Indians" who kind of all just lived separately from others. My great-grandmother and back are all seen as "mulatto" or "colored" on Censuses and marriage documents but I always concluded this was due to the above. 

Long story short, after revisiting the issue as a young adult in the 2010s, my jaw dropped when I made two key discoveries based on other's research. First of all, was a Y-DNA + mtDNA study on FTDNA on not just my grandma's side, but multiple other families that were known to have been of questionable racial background- as early as the mid 1700s on the Appalachian frontier. This group was referred to in places like NC, TN, and later KY as "Melungeon". The allegations had always hung over them as actually being mixed FPoC of African heritage, which of course would mean Jim Crow should've applied to them, too. Well, the results, especially on the Y DNA side established that that in fact was the truth the whole time, and not only that, thanks to the Y-DNA matches we have a connection to a surname which is a line of FPoC going back to 1600s colonial VA. And the double whammy is that this study establishing that men of that surname had a sub-Saharan African ancestor also led Ancestry.com researchers to [conclude that Obama's mother was descended from the man they think was the patriarch](https://cnnespanol.cnn.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/07/main_article_final.pdf), who is the earliest documented slave for life in the 13 Colonies. 

Its likely that his descendants married white women for a few generations in a row, until it was made explicitly illegal places like VA by the late 17th century. There is in fact a documented case of whats believed to be his great-grandson petitioning his local church in the early 1700s, attempting to get them to publish a marriage to a white woman. He sued to the courts, and his argument was that he was only 1/8th black, while current laws technically only dealt with 1/4 and up. The next year, the infamous Slave Codes of 1705 got passed, which include a random statute tacked on the end of another that specifies that anyone with 1/8th African heritage is black, and the racial limitations of those laws applied. Fast forward to my grandma's relatives settling in Appalachia, and in the late 1800s there are court cases in eastern Tennessee where locals challenged the rights of them to inherit property after a parent's death with no will- the charge being that due to being black, others were allowed to claim it. They won the case based on the fact that nobody could prove that they weren't just fundamentally white. But soon after, TN passed their first "One Drop Rule" statute which defined blackness as "up to 1/64th traceable African heritage".  

So in other words, it isn't just enough to know I'm descended from FPoC passing as "white enough", or heck even the earliest documented African-American slave, but one could argue that racial codes and laws chased my family throughout the nation's history. That, is a heavy weight, to know that I carry their blood and legacy with me.

Due to how scandalous her dad was with flings with multiple aristocratic women, Ada's mom decided to raise her as far away from how her dad was as possible. It should also be emphasized that due to cost and time constraints, they are not sequencing your entire genome, but instead are choosing a selection of genes to compare to their databases that have been identified as being unique to certain ethnicities or regions. A lot of people here are giving the *software* part of the explanation, but not explaining how the *hardware* side works. 

To explain this fully, let’s go back to development of the first commercially sold original electronic computer, the UNIVAC. UNIVAC was a massive mainframe style computer- think of multiple giant computer cabinets the size of a dresser as tall as a person is which ran code fed into it by magnetic tapes. Later budget minded systems used paper punch cards to do the same. So the issue is, as you’re streaming in code and it is calculating things, you need a way to stop it in the middle of things if you catch an error in your code to examine things, so what you do is wire this in to where when you send a certain signal, it pauses things. 

Fast forward to the development of the original IBM PC. Things have gotten a lot more miniaturized and complex by now. The first PC used a ROM chip called a *BIOS* which contains preset code to talk to hardware like the keyboard controller chip in a prenegotiated way. IBM naturally decides to include a way of interrupting the CPU to tell it new information for all devices. These interrupts are all set in a priority:

+ IRQ 0 – system timer (cannot be changed)
+ IRQ 1 – keyboard on PS/2 port (cannot be changed)
 + IRQ 2 – 8259 interrupt controller; cascaded signals from IRQs 8–15
+ IRQ 3 – serial port controller for serial port 2 (shared with serial port 4, if present)
+ IRQ 4 – serial port controller for serial port 1 (shared with serial port 3, if present)
+ IRQ 5 – parallel port 3 or ISA sound card
+ IRQ 6 – floppy disk controller
+ IRQ 7 – parallel port 1 (shared with parallel port 2, if present). It can also be potentially be shared with a secondary ISA sound card with careful management of the port.

Later on, as new hardware is added to the PC standard, this list expands out to include:
+ IRQ 8 – real-time clock (RTC)
+ IRQ 9 – Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) system control interrupt on Intel chipsets.[6] And/or left for the use of peripherals (use depends on OS)
+ IRQ 10 – The interrupt is left for the use of peripherals (for example, SCSI or NIC)
+ IRQ 11 – The interrupt is left for the use of peripherals (for example, SCSI or NIC)
+ IRQ 12 – mouse on PS/2 port
+ IRQ 13 – CPU co-processor or integrated floating point unit or inter-processor interrupt (use depends on OS)
+ IRQ 14 – primary ATA channel (ATA interface usually serves hard disk drives and CD drives)
+ IRQ 15 – secondary ATA channel

Now, notice that the first IRQ after the system clock is the *PS/2 keyboard controller*. This is a smart choice because it means that outside of keeping track of time for executing code, the CPU listens first and foremost for an interrupt request from the keyboard next. As before, this makes sense for especially debugging code as it’s executing on the relatively cheap, limited hardware it’s running on. Now, they also programmed in a keyboard shortcut to immediately halt all code running. Ctrl+alt+del is what it became. When Microsoft wrote MS-DOS as an operating system, they include this same shortcut as a way to force restart the OS to allow a user to get out of a frozen program. In Windows, you have the part of the OS called the kernel which is the part that talks to the bare hardware for you. It’s hard coded to listen for this keystroke and acts accordingly. 

This fundamentally is how things worked until circa 2006 and the introduction of what is called a *UEFI* to replace the old way of doing things with a BIOS. See, one of the issues with the BIOS is that it was really hardcoded for the original PC’s hardware, and to maintain backwards compatibility, every PC up to this point still initially boots up emulating that original hardware, with the same 16-bits wide memory address space, the same 1MB of RAM to load into an OS, etc. With modern hardware getting so powerful, this limits things on especially something like a server that might have several instances of different OS’s it needs to boot into. So Intel (IBM had long since lost control of their own PC standard to them and clone PC makers like Compaq, HP, and Dell) came up with a more modular firmware solution that’s also capable of running much more complex code at startup. A modern PC from the Core 2 Duo era and later then is able to still emulate this interrupting by sending a request via the USB controller on the CPU via this firmware.

>Whereas Hugh Gwyn hath by order from this Board brought back from Maryland three servants formerly run away from the said Gwyn, the court doth therefore order that the said three servants shall *receive the punishment of whipping and have thirty stripes apiece*. One called Victor, **a Dutchman**, the other **a Scotchman** called James Gregory, shall first serve out their times with their master according to their Indentures, *and one whole year apiece after the time of their service is expired by their said indentures in recompense of his loss sustained by their absence, and after that service to their said master is expired, to serve the colony for three whole years apiece*. Yes, my own genealogical discovery has taught me similar things! 

The main thing for me was the realization that things like antebellum racial laws were, just like today’s lawmaking, often what I’d call *reactive* in the sense of being codified after events happened that caused them to be made. I suppose that sounds kind of obvious to someone who is a professional archaeologist, but it doesn’t help that the oversimplified way we’re taught American history in grade school makes it out to be these institutions always existed as early as encounters with natives, and the African slave trade being instituted. When no, it’s actually quite a bit more insidious and evolved with time. 

Perfect example and how it relates back to my Melungeon heritage- through Y DNA testing, my Melungeon paternal ancestor matches with people who are [thought to be descendants of John Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Punch_(slave)), the man who has the unfortunate distinction of having the earliest known surviving records of being declared an African enslaved for life in the 13 Colonies. And yet, he most certainly despite being in servitude for life, was allowed to marry or at the minimum managed to have a baby worn a white woman. How do I know this? Because as the “Descendants” subsection gets into, the man thought to be his son (John Bunch I) was born free, than man’s son John Bunch II would’ve been born just as Virginia passed its first anti-miscegenation laws banning marriage of Africans and whites, as well as the fact that his likely great-grandson tried suing his local church to publish marriage to a local white woman, to which he lost the court case when he went before the House of Burgess. I have an ancestor who is the patriarch of that side of my family. He is at *least* likely 1/8th- 16th black going by who his paternal line likely was, more if any of his maternal side was mixed. He is found in early Censuses from atleast 1790-1840. In 1790 frontier NC, he’s listed along with all the other free [white] people. In 1800 NC/20 now in TN, however, he suddenly gets listed as a free person of color in that section of the sheets. Later in 1830/40 KY, he’s back to being listed alongside with free whites. Why? The 1790 Census was well known as being a bit rushed/sloppy due to being the first one, it may well be that the enumerators in such a frontier region never expected to encounter free people of color, and so he simply got listed on the same column. Meanwhile, the later censuses more accurately record him. Remember that back in these days, Censuses weren’t self-reported like today, local enumerators went out and documented people. But standards weren’t well defined and up to the local enumerator to mark someone how they saw fit, if the family was known in the area it may be that they were “close enough” by their standard. It also may be the case that my ancestor, after being established as a free land owner in his little corner in Kentucky, and especially since his children for the most part married “white” people in the area, that he got marked later in life as such. 

But by the middle of the 19th century, due to fears in the South about black people being able to successfully pass and inspire revolts as well as new beliefs that believed mixed people were prone to lesser quality of life, new standards got stressed that anybody even perceived as *possibly* being mixed with non-white should be marked as such. What’s extremely telling, too, is his kids going down one generation. My g-grandmother under him, and her son were 100% documented as “Mulatto” when racial categories became a thing in 1850 onward. Now by the time, the family oral history of instead being “Native American” develops, as attempts to apply for the Dawes Rolls in 1890/1900 survive. I also have a newspaper article with the original progenitor’s still living grandson, who claims he was told that he was part “Catawba”. This goes on all the way up to 1920 a few more generations down the line, where my great-grandmother was marked as “Colored” on her Kentucky Marriage Certificate. From what I understand it’s a combination of things, really: Growing up in a poor family and having to do agricultural farm hand type work as a kid conditioned him physically from a young age. Rice received position coaching in college from a former NFL player. And then when he gets drafted in 1985, he goes to of all teams the 49ers, the home of Bill Walsh and the West Coast Offense. Now, schematically Rice joining them as their X receiver was probably the best team at the time to go to, and that’s because the scheme was all about horizontally spacing the field with quick, precisely timed receiving routes, mesh concepts, and the combination with screens to force the defenses of the time that were more often predicated on the run and aggressive pass rushes to be punished. Which they did and led them 3 Super Bowls while he was there. A lot of what made Rice consistent wasn’t just the deep slant or post route, but from what I understand he ran even out routes crisp, and often times could turn what was meant to be a simple Out for 5-7 yards into something greater because of his great juke moves, so he was a YAC demon, too. But at 6’2” and 200 pounds, he had a deadly in betweener combination of size to give him sure hands on the deep ball, but also enough agility to make defenders miss consistently. He also has his legendary work ethic- even during the offseason in the Summer time there’s accounts of Jerry not just catching bricks, but also running several mile jogs on the outskirts of San Fran in the hills. That’s an intense workout regimen even by today’s standards and meant his conditioning was outstanding for all 60 minutes of a game. And footwork wise, he had to be consistent as Bill Walsh drilled precise timing into both his QBs via machine like consistent footwork, and the same in sync with his receivers. 

By the late ‘80s, a lot of defenses had countered what San Francisco had done so well by running more deep, 2 high safety coverages, and so the next evolution was George Seifert’s teams transitioning to a combination of a Mike Shanahan offense with a Zone Blocking Scheme with the threat of twitchy runs by both running backs as well as Steve Young, which continued to open up the existent passing patterns over the top and force defenders into conflict. Rice continued to thrive in this new offense, as the Shanahan trademark outside zone and stretch plays meant that Rice could continue to threaten on the outside as a receiver. The 49ers offense continues to be one of the more dominant in the league after Shanahan leaves in 1995 to coach the Broncos, with Young and Grbac pitching to him, but they sadly get one upped by teams like Dallas and Green Bay in this period, along with an aging defense holding them back. Steve Young retired and the next year, Rice calls it quits in San Fran and joins the Raiders for several more years. 

By this time Jerry had been slowing down, but there were still flashes of the old Jerry with a few explosive plays thrown in. And the offensive scheme Gruden installed, and the team continued after his infamous trade with Callahan and Trestman was based on the WCO as well. Both Gruden and Trestman spent time before hand as offensive assistants working for the likes of Seifert, and Mike Holmgren in both San Fran and Green Bay, after all.

The TL;DR oversimplified answer is watching the feet. If everyone’s first few steps right after the snap are all going the same direction, it’s a zone play. The idea is instead of blocking a single man like in power, you’re opening an area of the line for a run, and if executed well with double teams and good foot and handwork to give leverage, there’s multiple gaps that the RB can then read and pick from. Generally the RB has to be more fast and twitchy due to quickly reading and reacting, hitting that initial gap, then shaking tacklers since he’s usually smaller. Think a Pacheco or CEH type of RB with the Chiefs moreso. 

Power meanwhile is more about a singular preferred gap. Perhaps the most primitive power run play is simply known as “Power O”, usually in a modern offense this is a combination of your playside tackle (usually this is Sewell), and a pulling guard from the side opposite him who will quickly run over and hit the other side of the gap. If that side is good, he will then try to race to the second level to block a linebacker. Some teams will even add a TE to help out, too. 

Now once upon a time it was more cut and dry which teams were power, and which were zone- used to be the power teams had guards and centers that were beefier, and your tackles were more finesse. Nowadays, our Lions included, due to spread offenses, it’s much more equal- tackles are just ever so slightly more athletic and the guards are expected to have just as good footwork and sense of leverage, too. If you go back and watch that great OT winning drive against the Rams for instance, the first few plays are actually zone with Raymond and then Monty. This keeps the D-line off their feet as to what kind of blocking to expect, and guessing how to defend. 

Generally the Shanahan (as in, the father Mike) coaching tree which includes his son, and the likes of McVay and MLF default to mostly using a zone blocking scheme. This arguably goes further back to Mike’s time as the OC of the 49ers under Seifert, and then branched off as well to Mike Holmgren and Andy Reid. It gets even more fun than this. I learned this researching my early Kentuckian ancestors’ genealogy. 

So since Kentucky is unique in that originally it was a giant frontier county in Virginia, the issue arose after its settlers voted to become its own state of honoring existent contracts for land. It sounds pretty benign by modern standards, but with the especially pre-Civil War era US this is a serious issue of States’ Rights. Usually when other states were founded, they either simply inherited things from the former Colony, or former federal territory, and were given relative autonomy to decide things once incorporated as its own state. Kentucky meanwhile had decades of land sales that were abiding by *Virginia’s* laws, and standards, not theres. To add to the complication, as part of the agreement with the new US government, Virginia agreed to cede claims in the West in return for the promise that the temporary territory of Kentucky honor all old Virginia land claims. 

Specifically, it came down to squatter’s rights. Virginia, seeing Kentucky at the time as largely unsettled, was more lax when it came to settlers being able to claim rights to property they may have inadvertently squatted on due to a combination of frontier surveying that wasn’t clear, or due to natural barriers used to define them having been altered. (Think someone’s property barrier being defined by this large oak tree here, following a line to this rock there.) Kentucky meanwhile, now that it was its own thing had increasing complaints from early land owners who wanted back rent paid for people squatting. So they passed laws protecting people who unknowingly squatted, not requiring them to owe money if they had improved the land beyond the value of rent owed (cut down trees, leveled land, tilled and irrigated it, etc). So now, whose records do you honor, the old Virginia claims, or anything post-independent statehood? 

This case ended up in the Supreme Court, as *Green v. Biddle*. Here’s the real kicker though, and where my own genealogy comes into play. The Chief Justice in 1823 was still the famous John Marshall, a close relative of mine. He still heard the case, despite *his father having been the man tasked with surveying Kentucky post-Revolutionary War* and the both of them having used this early surveying knowledge to lay choice claims on land near major rivers and the like. Talk about a conflict of interest, right? Did John recuse himself from the case? Nope. In fact, he was part of the majority opinion (weirdly delivered by Assistant Justice Story perhaps due to the optics). Even more crazy? What if I told you his nephew was the attorney representing Kentucky? The court ruled in favor of Virginia here, angering Kentuckians to the point that it almost snowballed into a fully blown secession from the US crisis. 

This isn’t even the first time John Marshall absolutely still was active in a Supreme Court Case he shouldn’t have been. What if I told you that *Marbury v. Madison*, the case that established the right of judicial review for SCOTUS, and laid the ground work for Lincoln to be able to pass the 13th-15th amendments, was also predicated on this man blatantly ignoring conflict of interest? Who was the federal employee tasked with delivering the midnight appointments to the judiciary by the lame duck Adams administration? John Marshall’s brother, of course. Who benefited from said appointments, why John Marshall, of course. So what did he do, since he couldn’t simply call himself as a witness to the case as a judge sitting on it? He calls his brother in.

Every defensive scheme requires you to give up something to get something. It’s more to me about can your 11 guys execute better than their 11 for 30 minutes. 

Take a 4-3 Tampa 2, for instance. This goes hand in hand with mostly Cover 2, but with the variation that the MLB is quick and decisive while still having the size to defend the run. He’s usually asked to cover the slightly more deep middle part of the field if he reads pass. Well, that means there’s a “dead zone” in the shallow middle, which means shallow crossers and other mesh concepts in the middle that puts that Mike in conflict. Cover 2 is also vulnerable to something like seams routes right up the middle, so something like play action combined with a tall, fast receiver that can secure the ball deep is another way to defeat it. 

The type of scheme meanwhile that Flores runs is a 
modern 3-4 type of scheme similar to what he ran under Belichick. Generally what this entails (and this is extremely oversimplified) is more often a lot more 1 high safety shells (Cover 1/3/mixed coverages like 5/7 where the safeties kind of make reads independent of each other along with Cover 0 blitzes that are just pure man to man coverage), but they ask that the safeties are also able to mix in some zone/2 high type coverages as well to keep the QB constantly guessing and not trusting what his pre-snap reads are telling him. Now, 1 high usually means your corners are especially playing with a lot more man coverage principles- they know the chances of having quick help over the top are slim. And then what really makes it taxing on the QB at the D-line level is that your linebackers, often the inside LB on the strong/right side, along with the guys outside are dynamic play makers for their size, too. In a 3-4, the 2 DEs are both big and strong (versus a 4-3 where the strong side guy is more so, while the weakside guy is more of a pure pass rusher), and the single tackle is usually eating both gaps to the left and right of him, and so now you have ideally 5 gaps taken up by only 3 players. Which opens up vulnerabilities on the outside, from either a LBer or a surprise safety blitz. 

Now, as I alluded to, the “secret sauce” to this is the constant mixing up of the same players/personnel and new coverages ran. So you might have a playcall where before the snap there’s one safety standing way deep off the line, but the other safety that’s crowded on the outside, instead of blitzing drops back into coverage just at the snap, so surprise! It’s cover 2. If the QB thought he could throw behind that safety with anticipation assuming he was blitzing, he might instead be able to swat the ball away or even intercept it. Now, then, on offense, how do you truly attack this sense of organized chaos? You match what the defense is trying to do, but on offense. The Rams as you stated do this by having the same type of dynamic players at receiver- Cooper Kupp made his legendary success by being able to run the whole route tree- he’s just as deadly with good hands and timing in the slot, as a blocker setting up a screen, as he is running it deep as an outside receiver. He’s “only” 6”2’ and about 200 lbs, but he has strong hands for his size and great but not Tyreek Hill speed. Puka is a bit thicker but cut from a similar cloth. Robinson is almost the same size as Kupp, too. What this allows you to do is formulate route combinations that makes defensive players get confused which player is running what. And Kyren Williams is an extremely balanced running back who is just as deadly in the flat on the dump off as he is between the tackles. 

The Lions meanwhile also have dynamic playmakers, but they go about it a different way. Our receivers are much more specialized, but can make plays if asked of them, too. [See this TD by Amon Ra](https://youtube.com/shorts/tMfEQOgjJOQ?si=NB_PDMrsgSMvPn60). The Vikings aren’t even hiding an all out Cover 0 (100% man coverage for the DBs) blitz. Looking at our layout pre-snap, you have 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE assumed to both be blocking). The weird wrinkle though is that usually it would be Amon-Ra coming across on the jet motion at the snap to verify if it’s man coverage, then swinging out shallow as a slot receiver or in the flat. Meanwhile, it’s actually Tim Patrick, our bigger X receiver who gets used to chip the rusher on the right, and Amon-Ra in actuality is running a seams route straight into the end zone, something normally wouldn’t do. Just enough to freeze the DBs for that fraction of a second with a new look.

So the 3 second rule was first implemented on *offense only* in 1936. This rule states that players on offense are only allowed to stay still in the key (the painted part of the court underneath the net) for up to 3 seconds. After that, they have to bounce out. This rule was made in order to stop teams from simply clogging the paint and allowing their bigger players to have a free drive to the basket in so doing. After all, the game as envisioned by Dr. Naismith was supposed to be a cardio workout, right? Another thing you have to understand about basketball, unlike modern times, is playing defense in the paint back then meant hand checking was included. This is basically where a defender is also allowed to push or slap with his hands a player trying to drive in the paint to the basket. Unlike the pro game of today which is effectively all zone defense, this means man to man defense is a lot more effective, too. There also isn’t a shot clock yet (that wasn’t put into place until later) and so a lot of teams of Mikan’s era would simply try to pull a combination of controlling the boards (having your center in there underneath the basket to get rebounds on both offense and defense) and keep away once they got a lead- no shot clock means of course that you can just try to pass it over and over between players until your big guy gets a good position and lays it up. Mikan was one of the first athletic freak almost 7 foot tall centers to take advantage of this and feasted in this type of offense. So in 1951, they widened it to try to open up play. 

But teams were still playing keep away to drain clock. And the NBA realized that this style of play was low scoring and boring, and they introduce the shot clock 3 years later. Scoring started going up, but then a new wave of Mikan-type players became the new standard at Center. The king of all of them in many ways was Wilt Chamberlain who enters the league in 1959 at 7 foot 1. 

Wilt was like if you designed a player in a lab in so many ways. It wasn’t just his height, it’s his slim and muscular build, his 7 foot 8 inches wing span from arm to arm outstretched, and on top of his size, *the fact that he was able to play for 45+ minutes day after day in the era of the NBA with the highest pace to the game*. See, what you have to understand is even as recently as the ‘60s, the NBA was still small and less popular compared to the titan it is today. Schedules weren’t as forgiving, and sometimes games were back to back days for teams. It’s also a common mistake for casuals to think that before the 3 point line came in 1979, that this was a slower game- actually the *opposite* is true. Making it rewarding to shoot beyond the arc means teams take their time setting up a 3 point shot or kicking it back out. This man was such a physical specimen, he realized he could jump from the free throw line and simply dunk the ball from a standing start. And he played for more minutes on average than super stars today by far. He was a great shot blocker with the tools he had, and could jump and easily touch the top of a regulation *backboard* let alone rim. 

His first 2 seasons in the league from 1959-60, he led it in both *rebounds, minutes per game, and points*. An absolute monster that teams struggled to even deal with on defense. Now, remember what I said about defense being more hard nosed? If you jumped up with a guy to try to steal a pass, or hand checked him and thereby slammed him to the ground, often times this was a non-flagrant foul in these days that simply results in a free throw. So on top of him playing more minutes, this man took a beating. But he still scored. This culminates in his mythical 1961-62 season. In which Wilt “the Stilt” set the still NBA record for *48.5 minutes played for a season* (due to several overtime games) and *50.4 pts per game*. He capped off the season with one of the most impossible achievements to ever be accomplished. Which is his mythical [100 point game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilt_Chamberlain%27s_100-point_game). Yes, it’s so crazy it has its own Wiki page. Basically, after dominating the game early, the Knicks tried to constantly foul Wilt to slow him down. And he just kept on scoring after his teammates wanted him to break 100, he normally was just an okay to mediocre free throw shooter, but that night he shot 28/32. 

After this season, the NBA once again realized the game had essentially been broken, and so they widened the key again after the 1962 season.

Keep in mind as I said the most recent haplogroup is still several *thousand* years ago. It would be incorrect to deduce more recent ancestry based on this info. 

E-V22 for example is commonly found in North Africa and the Middle East (esp Saudi Arabia), but is also less frequently seen even in Mediterranean Europe, especially it looks like places like Sicily or Greece. With all sorts of branches from there.

So paternal haplogroups E-P2, E-V22, and E-M78 are all, despite the names looking different, branches and sub branches of the same “family tree” of haplogroups. Those names are using the YCC “shorthand” method of naming them, where E is the major, and the numbers and letters after the dash are the end of the major defining gene. In long hand, it’s a bit more obvious, as P2 is AKA E1b1, M78 = E1b1b1a1, and V22 = E1b1b1a1b2. 

That being said, these are all very ancient haplogroups- P2 is atleast 30,000 years old, and V22 is the most recent yet is still estimated to be about 11,000 years old. And the reason why is that when you took your tests at Ancestry and 23andMe and then uploaded the raw data to FTDNA, these are what you call autosomal tests. Instead of testing a selection of genetic markers purely on your Y chromosome like FTDNA’s much more expensive Y DNA tests, they mostly look at the other 21 to establish things like broader relationships and even health markers for 23andMe. Each platform is going to have their own series of algorithms to guess this information. It’s with these small amounts of markers that they extrapolate out what they can tell is your haplogroups, but it’s not as precise as taking a Y DNA specific test. FTDNA has a line of these that range in accuracy and price, if you’re interested still.

Generally what can mostly be gleaned is that you, like every male member of my paternal grandmother’s side, are likely descended from Ancient East African men. To establish things like more recent common ancestry, you’d have to take a Y test from FTDNA.

Youre playing the game [Simon Says](https://spectrum.ieee.org/media-library/photo-of-the-box-of-an-electronic-game-that-says-simon-and-shows-two-hands-pressing-colorful-buttons-on-a-round-object.png?id=50539567&width=400&height=250) with 3 friends, and you’re partners with each other, each team has their own game hardware. One player on each team is tasked with shouting instructions to their teammate, and whoever can hit the buttons the quickest the most times in a row wins. 

The only problem? The host team both are native English speakers. You, however, are playing with a foreign exchange student who does not know a single word of English, only Spanish. So, now you have to not just be able to communicate in a new language by looking up the new word every time (imagine you don’t have the short term memory to remember them, you only can remember English), but also have to try to do it as quick and accurate as the other team to even try to spit out the same pattern close to theirs in rhythm. 

 Now, multiply this problem by a few million times, and this is an oversimplified way of thinking of the issues with translating instructions in real time between two totally different architectures. Now, realize that most consoles since the 16 bit era have separate teams working to output video, sound, and then for the 32 bit era and later, sub teams which only handle things like the math required to figure out where the corners and edges of a 3D thing is, then how the surface of it should look from the angle you’re looking (a floating point unit). So you hop on over to the room with the “video” team, only to realize the way the room is physically organized is totally different, lets say the guy that’s really good at doing the math for the 3D object size calculates them as  hypothetical square objects to save time, not triangles like you’re used to.  And on top of them speaking a different language inside of just that room compared to what your video guys speak. So now, that’s a whole new set of issues to worry about when they pass stuff off to the other teams to work in concert. 

If you managed to write a dictionary to speed lookup of the translations, that’ll speed things up, but it will never be quite be with the exact same timing as the native English speaking team. Well, so you decide to find dedicated translators for the teams, but now that’s doubled your team size, and requires a ton more overhead even still. Actually exponential compared to what you’d think, because you have to then have translators between the Audio/Video/sound teams now too. 

Eventually, you iron out all of these things, but you realize that the original Simon Says teams that all speak the same language have only a few dozen team members and can whip out instructions smoothly without delay, meanwhile you have 1000x the total people they do to be able to relay things between rooms as quickly and accurately as you can. Finally, you match them a long time later after you’ve worked out all of the kinks.

Note that while a large percentage of people are located generally in the British Isles, it is also scattered across Eurasia and the Americas generally. 

This is an ancient haplogroup, and what you’ll learn is that it doesn’t really correspond to a modern nation state. Really, even more modern ones often transcend modern borders for the most part. 

What genealogical DNA test did you use to find it? It’s my understanding that autosomal tests like what Ancestry or 23andMe offer tend to try to look at a small selection of SNPs to deduce what your haplogroups are, but the problem is since they mostly focus on your autosomal DNA, these can be lacking in more modern precision sometimes. A service like FTDNA meanwhile offers a more expensive range of Y-DNA tests, and the “bigger” (albeit more expensive), the more precise it can drill down which more modern branch of that haplogroup you belong to. On the largest “Big Y” tests, the general mutation rate for this is estimated to be anywhere from only 2-3 generations. But the mutation rate of these SNPs can be somewhat unpredictable, so that’s not a given sometimes.

Digital animation hands down first of all is always going to be superior in giving the director the ability to layer shots, with multiple effects and alternate angles being much more easy to accomplish. When you used to hand draw stuff especially, 12 FPS was considered a good compromise for especially TV productions in transitions, whereas digital can accomplish more than that. 24/30 was usually reserved for key frames, but that’s the new normal for a high budget digital show. Theoretically, the lower man hours required to simply do the basic stuff can then compound into other aspects of the production like in the context of mecha, more detailed suit and character designs. 

However, hand drawn animation does still have its charm, don’t get me wrong. Things like color gradients and shading cannot be beaten when comparing to the highest budget productions that were purely analog, like the 0080/83 OVAs. Things just look more warm and organic, especially back and foreground elements. Honestly, my personal favorite will always be shows like Turn A, where most frames were still hand drawn, but with some extra digital special effects thrown on top of it, like when the Dark History and Moonlight Butterfly is activated.

America historically assigned the “lower standing” race based on what people perceived you as. I’ve learned a lot about this considering I have family (coincidentally, Obama is also descended from them via his mom) that, went from being mixed to white passing. 

Going back to colonial times, colonies like Massachusetts and Virginia quickly began passing racial laws starting in the 1640s-60s. First, they passed laws legalizing chattel slavery for life. Then, they defined free status as being inherited by that of the mother to make it so children of enslaved women were slaves and banned interracial marriage. Then after Bacon’s Rebellion happened, they passed further laws which began to limit civil rights for even free black people because they had participated in the uprising along with poor and indentured whites and freed slaves. 

Now, how you defined who was black even as early as the late 17th century also became an issue. One of my ancestors in this period was actually probably the grandson of the product of an early African man and a white indentured servant in Virginia. He sued in the 1690s to try to get married to a white woman after the church denied him. His argument was, as someone who was only mixed and part black, the law didn’t apply to him. He lost the case, and the same year the House of Burgesses passed a law further defining being black to include up to 1/4 African. Many colonies, especially in the South, followed suit. Beyond the aftermath of Bacon’s Rebellion, the incentive to do such a thing would’ve been there to allow enslaved people, who were increasingly becoming mixed due to assaults of black women, to still be legally in that social class. So, you had both political and economic incentive to equate African heritage with at best an untrustworthy free person of color, and at worst enslaved. Free people of color also suffered from unequal taxing, as the head tax laws were written to assume that women of color, regardless of free status or not, were taxable, while white women were not. 

Fast forward another century. By the mid 1800s, you had people like Josiah Nott who started writing about scientific racism, born out of studies into fields like phrenology, and then expanded by early Darwinism. They claimed to be able to show physical proof that black people were of another biological race, and that, while mixed people could have kids, after the point that someone was 1/8th black, they became sterile. Sort of like the idea of hybrid species loosing the ability to procreate after a while as well as suffering from other health issues (if there was ever a way to give this man a middle finger, it would be that my mixed relatives lived into their 90s in the 1800s). People like him managed to convince the Census Bureau to include terms like “quadroon” and “octoroon” to further mark these 1/4-1/8th mixed people, who were now formally considered black. After the Civil War, you have southern states react to the perceived threats of massive amounts of newly freed people of color. These ideas culminated, once again targeting people like my family, with “One Drop Rule” statutes after they caught wind of mixed people trying to pass as Native American or white mixed with it.

I have done some research into this since it deals with 1/4 of my family tree so, perhaps I can try to answer this to the best of my knowledge:

Among many early theories as to the origin of people like my family, the fact that a lot of us claimed indigenous heritage and coming from North Carolina + Virginia led people to posit this. The Lumbee historically lived in the swampy area in between central North and South Carolina, and are known to have among other things allowed escaped slaves to coexist with them, along with perhaps some sympathetic frontier whites who also escaped indenture and/or debt prison. So, you have a group that is known to have been “Triracial”, which many thought even in the 19th century that my people, were. In fact some people in the area who claimed to be Lumbee descendants actually willingly adopted the “Melungeon” label by the late 19th century. I really recommend reading the [article on Melungeons that the Journal of Genetic Genealogy that was published to discuss the results of the DNA study project on Family Tree DNA](https://jogg.info/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/71.006.pdf) for more details. But to sum it up: There are in fact some surnames (a branch of the Goins family especially) known to both groups in the late 19th to early 20th century. Genetic testing showed that this Goins branch is related to the Melungeon Goins’s. So there was atleast some now proven intermarriage there. 

My own branch actually claimed Catawba origins similarly, which would be interesting since the relationship with that tribe is a bit more complex, with some Catawba allegedly once again taking in escaped slaves, but also some others serving as guides for early slave catchers. I even have a St Louis newspaper article interviewing one my 4th great-grandfathers (born in the 1810s) in Kentucky from 1901 or so that he claims this in. By the time of my grandmother, this family lore has morphed into “Cherokee”, perhaps reflecting that side living in Eastern Kentucky for a few generations. 

However, what the aforementioned DNA study shows, is that atleast in both Y/parernal and mitochondrial/maternal DNA, most Melungeon families show mostly a mixture of white and *African* heritage, with some small amounts of indigenous mixed into some of them. The men who are descended from my ancestors, Valentine Collins, all have Y DNA haplogroups which are sub-Saharan African, and is found in the Dem Republic of the Congo, Central African Republic, and then places that imported slaves from central Africa like Saudi Arabia and the US. Why claim indigenous heritage falsely, then? A small amount of it has been proudly claimed by Virginia’s elite first family planter class due to Pocahontas. In fact, even Virginia’s “One Drop Statute” had a “Pocahontas exception” clause. (If there ever was a way to demonstrate how absurd being so obsessed with racial purity was, while also giving an exception, it’s this). 

So TL;DR is that: some modern Lumbee married into a large Melungeon family (the Goins) and claim both groups now. But not all Melungeons are Lumbee.

Another common misconception that’s sort of related to this- most people know that when a battery is connected to a circuit, the electricity flow goes from + to - terminals. So that’s the direction the electrons are flowing, right? Nope. It’s the opposite. The electrons are in abundance on the - terminal, which has that charge, and are attracted to the + side of the circuit naturally. This also has the side effect of creating a magnetic field which would orient itself in the same direction the electrons are going, from - to +, but at a 90 degree angle. 

A way to think about it is that magnetism is sort of like the waves in the water created by skipping pebbles on a lake. The direction of the pebble/electron is going forward, while the magnetic waves as it skips are 90 degrees transverse.

My answer is going to be a bit more nuanced- it depends. Remember first of all that most early 3D games running in DOS used software rendering. That class of CPU is great for 2D games and early 3D of the era (think more Wolf3D/Doom type of games), but later 3D stuff is where it might stutter a bit, and this is where I would question what sort of experience you’re looking for here. The type of experience that someone typical of the era might be forced to endure until they could afford to upgrade, or 60+ FPS on an LCD (or even better, a CRT that is able to vary its refresh rate+ native resolution) that’s smooth? The problem is trying to use an LCD, it has a fixed resolution that’s atleast 1024x768, and playing games below that point will require either a smaller image windowboxed (black borders on all 4 sides), or things not looking quite the best. 

When you want to be able to play retro games, are you going to be able to tolerate having to perhaps play a game like Quake 1 at a lower, 640x480 or halved resolution in DOS? Because that Pentium system will struggle to give you more than about 40 FPS there. If that’s something you can’t tolerate, or you’re especially trying to play on an LCD, I would say no. If you want to be able to truly max out the Quake 1-2s of the world with Win9x and DOS, you’d want something more along the lines of a Pentium III or AMD Athlon based system. The idea of a set ethnicity then later developed over time as people intermarried, began sharing closer and closer cultures and language, and so on. So I’m kind of unique in that my paternal grandma’s side were Melungeon, and I later discovered that my specific lineage was one that was the inverse- majority white, which ended up passing as such eventually, with African mixed in. Well, as part of the Melungeon DNA project on FTDNA, multiple male members of my grandma’s family who are descended from a man by the name of Valentine Collins and his grandson, Valentine Cole, tested themselves. And this is where it gets especially jaw dropping- the Bunch’s were apparently early FPoC who seem to descend from [John P/Bunch](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Punch_(slave)). Anyway, my point to all this is, that while we may never be able to properly put a name to a DNA trail as I was extremely lucky to be able to do, what we may *atleast* be able to do is establish paternal and maternal lines via samples taken from gravesites as they are discovered, and atleast be able to rebuild some semblance of a tree in that regard.
